title: Toward the Sunset
subtitle: Five Days with Thoreau's Walking for Finisterre and Muxía

spans.t: This is a small book for a short road. It has five days, one to read on each day of a walk, and it is made to go with the walk from Santiago de Compostela to Finisterre and Muxía: the road that leaves the cathedral city and goes west to the Atlantic coast. The CaminoPlus catalogue gives the route as ~90 km, measured to Finisterre. The figure is approximate, so check the current route before you go. If your walk takes more than five days, rest for a day or read one day twice. If it takes fewer, read two on a long evening. The book will not mind. It works at home too, with five mornings and five evenings and no boots at all.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
Walking

, an essay by the American writer Henry David Thoreau. The words are exactly his, in the English he wrote. Read them twice, the second time aloud if you can. He wrote for the ear, and the essay began as lectures.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Thoreau’s. It starts from something on the road, a verge, a wall, a bend, and lets the passage open it. It says plainly what he says, where it is hard, and what it might ask of an ordinary day. It is allowed to doubt, and sometimes to disagree.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.
A look back over the day you have just lived, with the morning’s passage in mind. It asks two or three gentle questions and is honest about tiredness.
A short prayer.
It is a prayer for those who pray and a wish for those who do not, so say it either way, and change any word that does not fit.

spans.t: Not a Christian book
Walking

is not a devotional book, and this is not a Christian reading. Thoreau was one of the New England writers called Transcendentalists, and here he writes about wildness and freedom. He uses the language of pilgrimage freely, as a picture. We have let him say what he says and made him say nothing more. People walk to the sea for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here.
The way west

The essay walks west, and so does the road. Thoreau says that when he goes out for a walk with no plan, he always ends up heading west, or a little south of west, and the essay finishes at a sunset. Finisterre and Muxía both lie west of Santiago, and the name Finisterre comes from the Latin for the end of the earth. The five days follow that line.

items.t: Day 1, leaving the house.
What it means to be ready to go.
Day 2, wildness and the open road.
Roads for business, roads for walking, and what is wild.
Day 3, the west.
Which way you turn when nothing decides for you.
Day 4, sauntering as a kind of pilgrimage.
A famous story about a word, and the idea inside it.
Day 5, the sunset and the shore.
What the edge of the land asks of you, and what comes after.

spans.t: The book cannot know which day of your walk is the last, so read the day that fits the day you are having. If you are tired, read the passage and the prayer and leave the rest for the morning.
Two things to know

Thoreau tells a well-known story about where the word “saunter” comes from. It is his story, and it is doubted. Day 4 says so plainly. The essay also carries the assumptions of its time, about the West, about Native peoples and about who is free to walk. We have chosen passages that do not rest on them, and where a day comes close, it says so, briefly. The next chapter has the rest.
On the road and at home
Read the morning part on a bench, in a bunk in an
albergue

(the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep), at a café table while the soup arrives. Then take the question with you for an hour. Read the evening part last, when the boots are off. At home, do the same with your tea and before bed.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road. Roughly, it means: may your Way go well.
Read slowly. The essay was written to be spoken, and it sounds better aloud.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man
Henry David Thoreau lived from 1817 to 1862, and spent most of his life in and around Concord, Massachusetts. He is best known for
Walden
, published in 1854, an account of living for a time in a small house he built beside a pond near Concord, and for an essay on conscience and the state now called
Civil Disobedience
. He earned his living in several ways, among them land surveying, and you can watch him at it in this essay. He died in 1862, aged 44.
We will not say more about his life than we can stand behind. His books are easy to find, and they speak for him better than a summary does.
The essay
Walking

began as lectures and was first published in 1862, the year he died. (The edition we used does not state a year, so the date is general knowledge, and we give it as that.) It is about 12,000 words long, roughly an hour of reading. It is a string of thoughts more than an argument: one idea leads to the next as one bend leads to the next, with side paths, jokes, and quotations from Latin, from Chaucer and from travellers’ books. It tells you at once what it is for. It begins: “I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute Freedom and Wildness”. It has no chapters, so the readings cite it as
Walking
and nothing more.

The essay says that walking is not exercise, taken like medicine at fixed hours, but “the enterprise and adventure of the day”. It says that walking takes leisure, freedom and independence, and that no money buys them. It says that a real walk is a kind of leaving. It says that the author, left to himself, turns west. Then it wanders through wildness, knowledge, names, literature and the future of a nation, before it ends, quietly, at a sunset.
Why it suits a pilgrim

It is a walking essay for walkers, and it is about direction. A road to the Atlantic coast goes the way Thoreau’s feet go, and a road that ends at the sea ends where his essay ends, at the edge of the light. It uses the language of pilgrimage throughout, and it is more interested in how to walk than in where. It is also short, funny and a little stubborn, and it can be read a page at a time.

It is not a gentle book, and it is not a humble one. Thoreau is sure of himself, he enjoys an overstatement, and he is not always fair. These readings do not try to make him humbler. They try to walk beside him.
Two cautions
The word “saunter”.

One of the essay’s best-known passages tells how “saunter” came from people on their way “à la Sainte Terre”, to the Holy Land. It is Thoreau’s derivation, and it is generally not accepted by etymologists. He gives another, from
sans terre
, “without land”, and that one is not accepted either. Day 4 uses the passage and says so in the reflection. We kept the story because the idea inside it does not depend on it.
The assumptions of its time.

The essay was written in the United States in the middle of the nineteenth century, and it carries the assumptions of its place. Its “West” is the American one, and it treats the westward movement of settlers, and the displacement of Native peoples by the farmer, as natural. It speaks of “savages” and “wild men” as figures of admiration, and of named peoples in ways we would not write today. The freedom it praises, to walk where you like and to have the leisure for it, was not open to everyone then, and it notices this only in passing. We have not tried to answer all this for him, and we have not hidden it. We chose passages that do not rest on it, and where a day comes close, it says so briefly and moves on.
The edition and the licence

This is an English original, so there is no translator. The text is the Project Gutenberg edition, ebook number 1022, which names no modern editor. Thoreau’s essay is a nineteenth-century text, and it is in the public domain. Every passage in this book was checked against that edition, word for word.

We changed nothing in the passages. We kept his spelling, his capital letters and his long dashes, and the American spellings of a New Englander. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. The choice of the five passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours, and they are original. Most of what we quote comes from the first half of the essay, and the last day comes from its closing paragraphs. The long middle of the essay is not here. It is still in the original for anyone who wants it.
Nothing of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied here.
What would you have to put down before you could simply go?
The passage

paras.t: It is true, we are but faint-hearted crusaders, even the walkers, nowadays, who undertake no persevering, never-ending enterprises. Our expeditions are but tours, and come round again at evening to the old hearth-side from which we set out. Half the walk is but retracing our steps. We should go forth on the shortest walk, perchance, in the spirit of undying adventure, never to return,—prepared to send back our embalmed hearts only as relics to our desolate kingdoms. If you are ready to leave father and mother, and brother and sister, and wife and child and friends, and never see them again,—if you have paid your debts, and made your will, and settled all your affairs, and are a free man; then you are ready for a walk.

spans.t: Reflection

The night before a walk, most of us make a list. It is mostly things to take: socks, plasters, a charger, a hat. Thoreau’s list runs the other way. It is a list of things to put down. Debts paid. A will made. Every affair settled. Father and mother, brother and sister, wife and child and friends, all left behind. Only then, he says, are you ready for a walk.

He is swinging a very large hammer, and he knows it. Near the start of the essay he warns that he means to make “an extreme statement”, and this is one. Hear it as half joke, half dare. A will, for an afternoon’s stroll! But the joke has an edge, and the edge is the point. Most of our walks are not leavings at all. They are tours that “come round again at evening” to the hearth they set out from, and half of every one is the same ground in reverse. We go out with a hand still on the door. He includes himself in that “we”, and fairly: most of the walks in his essay are afternoons near home.

Notice the flourish in the middle, the hearts embalmed and sent back as relics to desolate kingdoms. That is Thoreau enjoying himself. The whole essay goes like this: a big claim, a grin, and under the grin something he means. The word to listen for is the last one on the list,
free
. He opens by saying that he wants to speak for “absolute Freedom and Wildness”, and you can read everything after as an attempt to say what that would feel like on foot.

What he asks for is a spirit, not a distance. Even the shortest walk, he says, can be taken “in the spirit of undying adventure”. The difference is in what you are holding when you step out. Someone who has settled things, with nothing pulling at their sleeve, walks differently. They look up. They arrive in the field they are standing in, not the office they left.

The point of the list is not to be rid of your life. It is to put it somewhere safe, so that your attention can come with you. The debts and the will are a way of saying that nothing is left tangled behind you. You cannot carry a tangle and a pack at once, and by the second day the tangle may have shrunk to its true size.

Your road is a good place to try it, because it is not a circle. It leaves Santiago de Compostela and goes on towards the Atlantic coast, and each evening’s bed is a day further from your own door than the last. There is no hearth-side to come round to at six o’clock.
Now the hard parts, and there are three.

The first is the list. Hardly anyone is free in that way, and most of us should not want to be. There are people who would be frightened if you did not come back, and they are right to expect you. Nobody is asking you to walk out of your life. The word “never” belongs to the figure of speech. The mood is the part you can borrow.
The second is his word “crusaders”. It carries the memory of real wars, and he is using it only for a picture: someone who goes forth with nothing held back. Take the picture and leave the word.

The third is a plain doubt. If you wait until you are ready in his sense, you will not go. Nobody has paid every debt. The will is not made, the affairs are not settled, and there is a message you meant to answer a week ago. A walk has to begin anyway, in the middle of an unfinished life, and that may be the more honest kind of readiness.

So what does it ask of an ordinary morning? Something much smaller than a will. Pay one small debt: answer the one message that is sitting on you, or tell someone where you will sleep tonight. Choose one worry and put it down for the day, with a time to pick it up again if you still want it. Then go out as if this day were the whole of the walk. It is a decent way to spend a short walk, and a decent way to begin a long one. The list is not a hurdle. If you are reading this with your boots on, you have already passed the only test it sets.
For the walk

items.t: What am I still holding that I could put down for the length of this walk? Give it one word, and leave the word on the doorstep.

For the first ten minutes, walk as if you were not coming back this way. Look at each thing once, properly, the way you look at something you will not see again. Then let the trick go, and notice whether the rest of the day is any different. If you are walking with someone, tell them what you are doing and ask them to try it too.

spans.t: At the end of the day

The first evening has its own small sounds: boots set down by a door, a tap running, a phone searching for the one free socket. Wherever you are tonight, it is some way from the door you shut this morning. If you are reading at home, the same is true of the person who sat down at the desk. Let the day be over.

Look back at it as a leaving. What did you actually put down this morning? It may be nothing you could name. It may be one small thing: a message answered, a worry set on the table, an hour of “what if”. Say it to yourself in a sentence. Then ask the other question: what came with you after all? A plan for how the walk ought to feel. A comparison with somebody else’s pace. The office, which has a way of walking quietly behind. These are not failures. They are only heavier than they looked in the morning, and now you know where they sit on you.

One affair does need settling tonight, and it is not on Thoreau’s list: your feet. Look at them. Wash them, air them, and deal with a sore patch before it becomes a blister. If anything worries you, ask a pharmacist or a doctor. It is the most practical way to be ready for tomorrow.

Some of the day was good. Think of one stretch when you were simply where you were: a gate, a wall in the sun, a smell from a kitchen, a few minutes when you forgot to look at the time. It is probably short. It counts, and it is worth a second look now, while the day is still warm.

And some of it was hard, perhaps the first hour, when the pack argued with your shoulders, or the long middle, when you wondered why you had come. Name it kindly and set it down beside the good part. Neither needs a verdict tonight.

You may sleep badly. A strange bed, other people’s breathing, a day still humming in your legs: poor sleep on the first night is ordinary, and it does not mean the walk is going wrong. Lying still counts as rest even when it is not sleep.

A word about tiredness. A tired person is a poor judge of a whole walk. Tonight’s mood is not the book’s verdict on the road, or on you, and nothing has to be settled before sleep. The list of unfinished affairs will scroll once or twice behind your eyes. Let it scroll. By morning it will be shorter, or at least lighter, and the road will still be going west.
Questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I put down today, even for an hour, that I expected to keep holding?
Where did I walk as though I might not pass this way again?
Who is expecting to hear that I am well, and what would I like to tell them?

spans.t: A short prayer

Let me be where my feet are. Let what I left at home be safe without me for a night. May what I carry be only what I need. May the bed be warm and the evening kind. Tomorrow, let me begin again, lightly.
What would it be to take a road for its own sake?
The passage

paras.t: Some do not walk at all; others walk in the highways; a few walk across lots. Roads are made for horses and men of business. I do not travel in them much, comparatively, because I am not in a hurry to get to any tavern or grocery or livery-stable or depot to which they lead. I am a good horse to travel, but not from choice a roadster. … However, there are a few old roads that may be trodden with profit, as if they led somewhere now that they are nearly discontinued. There is the Old Marlborough Road, which does not go to Marlborough now, methinks, unless that is Marlborough where it carries me. … Life consists with wildness. The most alive is the wildest. Not yet subdued to man, its presence refreshes him.

spans.t: Reflection

Every walker learns two kinds of road. One is built to get you there. It is straight and surfaced, it has a line down the middle, and it is not interested in the fact that you are on it. The other is a track between walls or hedges that exists because people kept walking along it, and it goes on, patiently, because they did. A morning on each is a different kind of weather. On the first you hear engines. On the second you may hear your own boots, then birds, then, now and again, nothing at all.

Thoreau has views on the first kind. “Roads are made for horses and men of business.” He is in no hurry to reach any tavern, grocery, livery-stable or depot, and so he keeps off them and walks across lots, which means across fields, which means wherever his feet can find a way. He is, he says, “a good horse to travel”, though not, from choice, a roadster. A good horse to travel can go a long way without fuss. A roadster is a horse schooled to the highway. He claims the first and declines the second.

Then he does something more interesting than turning his back on roads. He praises one particular sort: an old road so little used that it has lost its purpose. His own Old Marlborough Road, he says, does not go to Marlborough now, “unless that is Marlborough where it carries me.” It is a lovely sentence, because it turns a destination into a result. A road with no business left in it is a road for walking, and where it ends is wherever it takes you.

A pilgrim road is an old road in that sense. Almost nobody needs it for speed. There are quicker ways to the coast, and most of them have a line down the middle. People walk this one for the walking, and for the sea at the end.

The last lines of the passage come from a different part of the essay, and they say what he is really after: “The most alive is the wildest.” It is easy to hear that wrongly on a road that thousands of feet have worn smooth. Thoreau does love a wilderness, but he finds wildness close to home as well: in a bog beside the village, and in a neighbour’s cow that breaks out of her pasture early one spring and swims the river, which he cheers. Wildness, for him, is whatever has not been wholly arranged for us: weather, hunger, a bird in a wall, a cow in a lane, and the animal part of the walker that wants water and a chair. It is what we have not yet been trained out of, and its presence, he says, refreshes.

A word about lots. Thoreau crosses fields because, in his time and place, he could. Later in the essay he says that the walker enjoys “comparative freedom” there, and he fears the day when fences go up. You are walking among people’s homes and livelihoods. Stay on the way. The narrowness of a pilgrim road is a courtesy to the people whose fields lie beside it, and keeping to it is the freedom you give them.
Where is it hard? In two places.

First, he is a little sniffy about roads and the people who need them, and most of us need both. Somebody has put a mark at the corner where you were about to be lost. That is no insult to wildness. It is a courtesy, and you can accept it and still keep your eyes open.

Second, “wild” is a risky word on a walk. It is no reason to walk where you cannot be seen, to ignore the weather, or to stay on the wrong side of a busy road. Where this way meets traffic, the sensible thing is to walk where you can see what is coming. Thoreau’s wildness lives in the field beside the road, not in the middle of it. The same goes for weather, which can change within the hour. Carry water and a layer for rain, and let the wild be a pleasure you have prepared for.
And a small honest doubt. Some days the wildest thing you want is a chair and a hot meal. That is allowed. It is wild in its way. Nobody arranged your hunger.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Give one stretch of the road no purpose at all. Not “the way to the next village”, just this lane, this wall, this wind. Let it be the place you are, and not the means to somewhere else, and see what the road has been saying while you were busy getting along it.
For the walk

items.t: Which part of today’s walk could I do for its own sake, with no part of me waiting to arrive? If none, which part could come closest?

Find something living that nobody planned: a bird, a weed in a wall, a cow at a gate, a cloud going a different way from you. Watch it for a full minute, sixty slow breaths if that helps, then walk on and notice how the road feels and whether you are walking any differently.

spans.t: At the end of the day

By now your feet know the road better than your head does. Tonight, look back over the day as a set of roads. Some stretches were the first kind, built to get you there: you walked them with your head down and a number in your mind, kilometres or minutes to the next place. Some were the second kind, a way that carried you. Which was which? It is not always the surface that decides. A paved lane can feel old, and a path through trees can feel like a corridor.

Then think about the wild, and begin with your own body, which is the wildest thing you carry. Tonight it is asking for water, salt, a hot shower, a chair with arms, a little silence. Give it as much of the list as you can. It asks without apology, and it is usually right.

Did anything else today refuse to be arranged? A change of wind, a shower, a smell, a sound you could not place, the mood of the afternoon. The body counts: its hunger, its limp, its surprising wish to sing or to lie down. None of it was on the plan. All of it was yours.

Somewhere today you were probably hurried by something: a bed to secure, a café before it closed, weather coming in. That is the road of horses and men of business, and you are allowed to use it. The only question is whether it took the whole of the day or only the part it needed.

Think, too, of the hard part, and give it a fair hearing. It may have been the length, or a road with no verge, or the plain monotony of putting one foot after the other. Say what it was. It does not have to be turned into a lesson. If it was a stretch where you felt unsafe, tell your host and ask about another way round tomorrow.

If you are reading at home, the same questions fit an ordinary day. Which of today’s roads were for business, and which for walking? Was there a lane, a park path or a bit of pavement that carried you? There nearly always is one.
If you can, step outside for a minute before bed. Look at what the evening is doing from the doorway: the light going, the smell of the ground, the first lit windows. Nobody arranged that either.

Tired walkers think in straight lines: food, bed, sleep. Before you lie down, spend a minute on a bend you liked. It is the part of the day that will not come back, and it takes no time to keep. Tomorrow’s road will have its own, and you will not know which until you are on it.
To take to sleep:

items.t: Where today did the road simply carry me, and where was I only trying to get somewhere?
What was the least arranged thing I met today, and how did it feel to meet it?
What would I give a little less hurry to tomorrow?

spans.t: A short prayer

May the road carry me where it will. May I be in no great hurry to arrive. Let something wild and small cross my path tomorrow, and let me stop for it. Let my feet be sure and my eyes be open. Let sleep come easily.
When nothing decides for you, which way do you turn?
The passage

paras.t: When I go out of the house for a walk, uncertain as yet whither I will bend my steps, and submit myself to my instinct to decide for me, I find, strange and whimsical as it may seem, that I finally and inevitably settle southwest, toward some particular wood or meadow or deserted pasture or hill in that direction. My needle is slow to settle—varies a few degrees, and does not always point due southwest, it is true, and it has good authority for this variation, but it always settles between west and south-southwest. The future lies that way to me, and the earth seems more unexhausted and richer on that side. … Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free. Thither no business leads me. … Every sunset which I witness inspires me with the desire to go to a West as distant and as fair as that into which the sun goes down. He appears to migrate westward daily, and tempt us to follow him.

spans.t: Reflection
On a waymarked road you hardly ever choose a direction. Someone has chosen it for you and put a mark at the corner. It is restful, and it can make you forget that direction is a choice at all.

Thoreau has to decide every time. He steps out of his front door with no plan and lets his instinct decide, and he finds, strange and whimsical as it may seem, that he always ends up heading south-west or west. He turns round and round, sometimes for a quarter of an hour, irresolute, and then the needle settles. It is a slow needle, and it varies a few degrees. But it never points east. “Eastward I go only by force; but westward I go free.”

Then comes a short sentence that holds a whole idea: “Thither no business leads me.” Free, here, may not mean without limits. It may mean without errands. Elsewhere he says that we go east to study history and the works of art, and west into the future. East is where the obligations are, and west is where he has nothing to do. That is one way to read it, and it is ours, not his, but it fits the way a walk feels around the third afternoon. The road has stopped being a list of things to get done, and has begun to be a direction.

There is a second thing in the passage, and it is easy to miss: “The future lies that way to me.” For Thoreau, direction is not only geography. West is where he expects something to come from. You may have set out from a change, a loss, a decision, a job that ended, and feel that the road leads away from one thing and towards something you cannot see. You do not have to know what. That the earth “seems more unexhausted and richer on that side” is a very honest description of a hope: not a plan, only a feeling that there is more over there.

The last lines of the passage reach for something older than Thoreau. Every sunset, he says, makes him want to go to a West as distant and as fair as the one the sun goes down into, and the sun seems to tempt us to follow. He seems to take it for an old feeling: in the same paragraph he adds that the ancients appear to have set their islands of paradise out there, in the west.
Your road has that direction in it. Both Finisterre and Muxía lie west of Santiago, on the Atlantic coast, and the name Finisterre comes from the Latin for the end of the earth,
finis terrae
. The CaminoPlus catalogue gives the road to Finisterre as ~90 km, a figure worth checking before you walk.

And here is the difference between you and Thoreau. His west never ends. Whenever he walks, there is more of it, further on. Yours does. There is a coast, and beyond it only water. A direction is something you can follow for ever. A destination is something you arrive at. Over the next days you may find that you are walking both: leaning west out of long habit, and going to a particular place, on a particular day, where you will have to stop.
Two cautions.

The first concerns the West itself. Thoreau’s is the American one. Elsewhere in the essay it grows into the march of a nation across a continent, and the settlers’ advance, and the displacement of the people already living there, are treated as natural, even as good. The land to the west was not empty, and to walk west was never an innocent thing for everybody. We have chosen a passage that stays with one man and his compass, and we do not ask you to carry the rest.

The second is smaller, and kinder. A needle that “varies a few degrees” is an honest one. Your road will not run due west either. Roads rarely do. This one will bend round hills and villages, as most roads do, and for part of an afternoon it may point somewhere else altogether. That is not a failure of direction. It is what a path does when it respects the ground.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? To notice which way you lean. Not only on the map, but in the day: towards the next meal, towards the next person, towards the end. And, once, to follow something just because nothing is asking you to.
For the walk

items.t: Which way am I leaning today, on the map and in my mind, and is anything leading me there that I have not noticed?

If the sun is out, watch your shadow. In the morning, walking west, it falls ahead of you. In the afternoon it falls behind. Notice the moment it changes sides. If it is cloudy, notice the wind and the light instead, and ask which part of the sky is brightest. If you are reading at home, find the west by the evening sun.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Somewhere around the middle of a walk, the road stops being new and starts to be a habit. Tonight, ask which way it led you, and not only on the map.

Think about what pulled you. The next village, the next meal, the sight of a bed, a walker just ahead whom you wanted to catch, or to avoid. These are small magnetisms, and they are fine. But there may also have been a quieter one, which you notice only when you stop: a wish to see how it ends. You may be able to name it by now.

Think about the hard part of today. It might have been the length, or the heat, or the rain, or a bend where the road turned away from where you wanted to go. Say it plainly, and then notice that you came through it.

And the good part: an easy stretch where the road and your legs agreed, perhaps with the light low in front of you, if the sky allowed it. A day has one of those more often than we give it credit for.

Thoreau draws the outline of his walks as a curve that opens to the west, with his house in the place where the sun would be. Home is the warm point you keep moving away from, and the pull of it does not stop. It may have been strongest this afternoon, or when you looked at your phone. That is allowed too.

As the end of a road comes closer, two wishes arrive together: to get there, and for it not to end. Both are fair. Hurrying to arrive and dawdling to avoid arriving are both ways of not being on the road. Whichever you feel, notice it without arguing, and tomorrow walk at the pace of the day and not of the end.

There is a question underneath all this, and you do not have to answer it tonight. Is it a place you are walking to, a direction you are walking in, or something you are walking away from? Grief, a change, a need to be out of a room: these are all good reasons to walk, and they point differently from a destination. Thoreau gives reasons for his west, but he also calls it an instinct, and an instinct does not always know its own reasons.

Before you sleep, find the west. If there is a window or a door, look at the part of the sky where the light went, even if cloud hides it. Tomorrow’s road lies in that direction, and it costs nothing to say good night to it.
Tired people steer by the nearest light. That is allowed. Tonight the only direction needed is the way to the bed, and the rest of the compass will keep until the morning.
Three questions for tonight:

items.t: What has been pulling me west, and what else has been pulling me that I have not named?
Where today did I follow something just because nothing was asking me to?
Am I walking toward a place, in a direction, or away from something?

spans.t: A short prayer

May I know which way I am leaning. May the light be kind at the end of the day. Let me follow the next small thing that calls me, and let it be good. If I am lost for a while, let me be lost gently. May my feet keep their direction while I sleep.

chapters.title: Day 4. Saunterers in the good sense

spans.t: What are you walking toward, even if you cannot yet name it?
The passage

paras.t: I have met with but one or two persons in the course of my life who understood the art of Walking, that is, of taking walks—who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering, which word is beautifully derived “from idle people who roved about the country, in the Middle Ages, and asked charity, under pretense of going à la Sainte Terre,” to the Holy Land, till the children exclaimed, “There goes a Sainte-Terrer,” a Saunterer, a Holy-Lander. They who never go to the Holy Land in their walks, as they pretend, are indeed mere idlers and vagabonds; but they who do go there are saunterers in the good sense, such as I mean. … Some, however, would derive the word from sans terre without land or a home, which, therefore, in the good sense, will mean, having no particular home, but equally at home everywhere. For this is the secret of successful sauntering. He who sits still in a house all the time may be the greatest vagrant of all; but the saunterer, in the good sense, is no more vagrant than the meandering river, which is all the while sedulously seeking the shortest course to the sea.

spans.t: Reflection
Thoreau tells a story about a word. It is a good story, and it is almost certainly not true.

The word is “saunter”. In his account it comes from idle people who roved the country in the Middle Ages and begged, saying they were on their way “à la Sainte Terre”, to the Holy Land, until the children shouted “There goes a Sainte-Terrer.” A saunterer, then, is a Holy-Lander. Those who never reach the Holy Land in their walks, he says, are mere idlers and vagabonds. Those who do are saunterers “in the good sense”.

Say it plainly: this is Thoreau’s etymology, and it is doubted. Etymologists do not generally accept it, and they see no link between “saunter” and the Holy Land. The origin of the word is usually called uncertain. He offers a second derivation, from the French
sans terre

, “without land”, and says he prefers the first, “the most probable derivation”. Neither is accepted today. So read the story for what it is: a metaphor, told by a man who likes a good tale. The idea inside it does not need the history to be true.

What is the idea? That the difference between a wanderer and a saunterer is not speed, or distance, or even religion. It is whether the walk is going somewhere in the walker’s own mind. Thoreau leaves the Holy Land undefined, which is the generous thing to do. For one reader it may be a church, for another the sea, a person, a rest, a quieter head. Whatever you put there, a walk that has one is a different walk from a walk that has none.

Notice, too, what he says before the story: that in his whole life he has met only one or two people who understood the art of walking, “who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering”. He means a way of paying attention, not stamina. A little later he adds, in Latin, that a walker is born and not made. We doubt it. You may find that a few days on a road teach you more of the art than you expected.

The second derivation gives the better lines. A saunterer would be someone “having no particular home”, and so “equally at home everywhere”. That will sound familiar to anyone with a pack on their back. You own what you carry. The bed changes every night. You are a guest in all of it, and some evenings the guest is comfortable and some evenings not.

Then the river. The saunterer, he says, is no more a vagrant than a meandering river that is, all the while, seeking “the shortest course to the sea”. It is a consoling picture for a winding path. A river’s bends are not a failure to go straight. They are the shortest way the ground allows. Your road bends round hills and through villages for the same sort of reason, and it is going to the sea.
Three things in the passage are hard.
First, he is unkind to the idle, roving poor of his own story, and the line does him no credit. Pilgrim roads have long relied on the hospitality of people who gave a bed or a meal to strangers.

Second, “equally at home everywhere” is a fine ideal and a difficult one. There will be an evening when you are at home nowhere: a strange bed, sore feet, a room full of other people’s sleep. It will not help to be told that you should feel otherwise. The ideal is a direction and not a test.

Third, “Holy Land” is a religious phrase in a book that is not religious. We have kept it because it is his, and because he stretches it so far that it fits any reader. If it does not fit you, put your own word in its place. A reader who is Christian, or of another faith, or of none, may hear it differently on different days, and that is all right.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? To let the road be crooked and not mind. To keep the point of the walk somewhere in view without staring at it. And to be a good guest: at home enough to rest, and light enough to leave in the morning.
For the walk

items.t: What am I walking toward today, even if I cannot name it? If nothing comes, let that be the answer for now. Some walks only show their Holy Land when you arrive.

For one hour, do not check the distance or the time. Let the bends be the way, as they are for a river, and notice how the walking changes when you stop measuring it. If you cannot resist, check once at the very end, and see how far you came without counting.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Tonight the question of home is a practical one. Where are you sleeping, and how much does it feel like yours? Some places take a person in at once: a clean sheet, a kind word, a chair that fits. Others need a night to warm up. Think about how it was to be a guest today, and about whoever played host, even if they were only a stranger who held a door.

Take a moment, too, over the pack on the floor. What did it hold that you used today, and what is only weight? There may be something you have carried for days and not touched. You do not have to decide tonight. But the saunterer with no particular home carries what the road asks for and not what the worry asked for.

Then think about the bends. What went the long way round today: a path round a field, a wait you did not plan, a wrong turn, a stretch that felt twice as long as the sign said? From here, which of them looks like part of the shortest way the ground allowed? You may find that some of them were the best of the day. You may find that none of them were, and that is honest too.

There may have been a moment when you felt at home nowhere. A strange town in the late afternoon, an unanswered message, a meal eaten alone at a table meant for two. It is part of the walk, and it passes. You do not have to turn it into wisdom. Put it down next to whatever was warm.

If a host was kind to you today, thank them once more in your mind. A roof and a bed are the oldest gift of any road, and the story of the idle beggars leaves out the people who put the pilgrim up. However far the sea is tonight, your river is still going to it.

A small exercise for the bed: name three things in the room that make it bearable. The light switch you can find in the dark, the window, the sound of a tap. Being at home everywhere is built of small things like these, one room at a time. Some evenings the Holy Land is a hot meal. If that is what lies ahead, then it is.

A tired saunterer is just a person who wants a shower. That is a perfectly good thing to be, and the Holy Land, whatever you have put there, will not mind waiting until you have had one. After that, eat something warm if you can, and let the day finish itself without any help from you.
Questions to sleep on:

items.t: Where did I feel at home today, and what made it so?
What was I walking toward today, even if I could not have said it aloud?
Which bend, delay or wrong turn now looks like part of the shortest way?

spans.t: A short prayer

May I be a good guest and a good host. May the road bend as it needs to, and may I not mind. Let me be at home in this bed tonight and light enough to leave it. Let the long way round be the right way for me. Let sleep find me quickly.

chapters.title: Day 5. The sun on our backs

spans.t: What do you do when the west runs out?
The passage

paras.t: I was walking in a meadow, the source of a small brook, when the sun at last, just before setting, after a cold grey day, reached a clear stratum in the horizon, and the softest, brightest morning sunlight fell on the dry grass and on the stems of the trees in the opposite horizon and on the leaves of the shrub-oaks on the hillside, while our shadows stretched long over the meadow eastward, as if we were the only motes in its beams. It was such a light as we could not have imagined a moment before, and the air also was so warm and serene that nothing was wanting to make a paradise of that meadow. When we reflected that this was not a solitary phenomenon, never to happen again, but that it would happen forever and ever, an infinite number of evenings, and cheer and reassure the latest child that walked there, it was more glorious still. … The west side of every wood and rising ground gleamed like the boundary of Elysium, and the sun on our backs seemed like a gentle herdsman driving us home at evening. … So we saunter toward the Holy Land, till one day the sun shall shine more brightly than ever he has done, shall perchance shine into our minds and hearts, and light up our whole lives with a great awakening light, as warm and serene and golden as on a bank-side in Autumn.

spans.t: Reflection

Light just before sunset does something no other light does. It comes in low and from the side, and it turns the ordinary into something nobody put there: a wall, a thistle, a wet road. Thoreau’s passage is an attempt to say what that is.

The scene is a meadow by the source of a small brook, in November, after a cold grey day. Just before setting, the sun finds a clear gap in the horizon, and the softest, brightest light comes across the dry grass. It is “such a light as we could not have imagined” a moment before, and the air is so warm and serene that nothing is wanting to make a paradise of the meadow. Then comes the thought that matters most. It was “more glorious still” when they reflected that this was no one-off. It would happen “forever and ever, an infinite number of evenings”, and would “cheer and reassure the latest child that walked there”.

There is comfort in that. A sunset is a small private event, and it is also something the world keeps on doing, whether or not anyone is there. You do not have to hold on to it. This evening it is yours, and tomorrow evening it will be someone else’s.

Now the doubt. Thoreau’s sunset was a gift: a grey day that cleared at the last moment. The Atlantic does not promise one. You may get cloud, or mist, or rain, and the sun will go down behind it all the same. The essay does not promise a sunset either, and the road was never for sunsets alone. If the sky is shut tonight, the day has not been wasted. And no one can be asked to feel awe on schedule. If you watch with other people and feel nothing much, you have not failed the sunset, and it has not failed you.

This is the day the west runs out. For four days Thoreau has given us a direction. At Finisterre or Muxía the direction meets the sea, and there is a horizon with no road in it. His own west does not end like that. Every sunset sends him on towards “a West as distant and as fair”, and he never has to stop. Yours does. So what then?

The essay answers with its last turn, and it is a quiet one. In the passage the sun is on their backs, “like a gentle herdsman driving us home at evening”. They are walking home. They are going east, away from the sunset, and yet the last sentence begins: “So we saunter toward the Holy Land”. The walk does not stop being a pilgrimage when the walker turns round. At the shore you will turn round too, and if you do it in the evening, the sun, if there is any, will be on your back. It is not defeat. It is the part of a walk that most stories leave out, the going home, and the essay says it still counts.

His last sentence is a hope, not a promise. The sun shall “perchance” shine into our minds and hearts, and light up our whole lives, “as warm and serene and golden as on a bank-side in Autumn”. We cannot promise a great awakening, and neither could he. But the light on a bank-side in autumn is on offer on any good evening, and it costs a walk.

One plain practical thing. If you go to a cape to watch the sun go down, plan the way back before the light goes, because you will return in the dark. Carry a light, keep well back from the edge of the rocks, and keep an eye on the waves, which can reach higher than they look. 112 is the European emergency number.
What does it ask of an ordinary day, the last one? To look once more at what is in front of you, properly, before the light changes. And to remember that turning round is also a way of walking.
For the walk

items.t: What would I like to look at once more, properly, before the light changes? Choose one thing, and give it the whole of a long breath.

Sometime today, stop and turn all the way round, once. Look at the road behind you, the same road seen from the other side, and let it be lit by whatever light there is. Then turn back and walk on. A road looks different from the other side.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Whether you are at the end of the road tonight or only at the end of the book, this is an evening for endings. Take them in order, gently.

You set out with a list of things to put down. You looked at roads and found two kinds. You turned west, or leaned that way, and followed something that pulled. You were a guest, again and again. Now the land has run out, or the pages have. There is nothing to prove tonight and nowhere left to get to.

You may feel a great deal, or hardly anything. Both are ordinary. You may weep at the sea, or eat a sandwich and look at it. Neither is a failure. If you keep a journal or send a message home, one line is plenty: where you are, what the light was doing, one thing you saw. If the water is near, listen to it for a minute. If it is far away, listen to whatever is.
Look back at what was hard. The long afternoon, the blister, the day you wanted to stop, the one you did not want to end. Say thank you to your feet. They did it, whatever else was going on.

And what was good? Not only the big things, if there were any. The ordinary kindness, the soup, the stretch where the walking became easy. Hold one of them for a moment before it fades into the general blur of a finished road, which it will. Remember the list on the first morning, with its small debts and the one worry you set down for the day. See whether it is still on the doorstep. You do not have to pick it up.

Think of the people who made the road possible: whoever marked it, whoever fed you, made the bed or opened the door, and the people who live beside it and let you pass. You will probably not meet most of them again. Say thank you in whatever way is left to you. And if the sea was grey, or the sunset did not come, notice any disappointment and let it be there. It does not cancel the road.

Then the practical question that follows every end: what are you taking home? Not objects. A direction you like to lean, a pace, a way of being a guest, one small thing you put down and have not picked up again. It is enough to know that there is a home to take it to. You may find that tomorrow feels flat, with no arrows to follow. If so, plan it gently: a long breakfast, a message to someone, a short walk in a direction you have not tried. The next chapter says more about going on.
Three questions, and nothing to prove:

items.t: What do I want to carry home from this road, and what am I glad to leave behind here?
When on this walk did I feel most awake?
Who do I want to tell about it, and what is the first thing I will say?

spans.t: A short prayer

May the light be kind tonight, wherever it falls. Thank you, road, for the long way round. Let what I leave here stay here, and let what I carry be light. May the way home be easy, and may I walk it awake.

You have come to the end of the road, or the end of the five days, or both. This book gives no certificate. It was meant as company for a short walk west, and a road has no use for a book once the land has run out, except to be remembered kindly.
So the only question left is what to keep.
Not everything. Nobody carries a whole book home. Choose three small things, one of each kind.

items.t: A direction.

Thoreau’s needle settled in the west. Yours may settle somewhere else. Notice which way you lean when nothing decides for you, and give it a little room when you are home. One evening this week, walk toward wherever the day ends for you, with no errand at all.
A line.

One sentence from the five days that stayed in your head. It might be “westward I go free”, or the gentler “unless that is Marlborough where it carries me”, or “an infinite number of evenings”. Write it on a card and put it where you will see it.
A practice.

One of the small things from the end of each morning: ten minutes of walking as if you were not coming back, a minute with something nobody planned, a shadow noticed, an hour without measuring, a turn all the way round. Pick the one that cost you least and helped most. Do it again tomorrow.

spans.t: If you can keep all three for a month, you will have kept more than most people keep from a week away.
How to go on

Go back whenever you like. The days are short, and they were written to be read more than once. A day that did nothing for you at the start may say a good deal on a grey Tuesday in March. Read them in another order. Read only the evenings for a week. Read the first passage aloud on a morning when you cannot get out of the door.
You might also read Thoreau himself.
Walking

is about 12,000 words, it is in the public domain, and you will find it at Project Gutenberg, ebook number 1022. Read the parts we left out with the same calm we have tried to keep. You will meet his jokes about knowledge and names, his fondness for swamps and, in places, assumptions that we named at the start and have not repeated. Some of it you will love, and some of it may make you wince. Both are fair responses to an essay that is more than a century and a half old.

He said he could not keep his health and spirits unless he spent “four hours a day at least” walking. Few of us have that. An hour is a good start. A walk to the end of your own road and back counts, and so does a walk to the end of the next one.

And be honest about what did not work. Some days will have rubbed. A passage may have asked for more than you had, or sounded too sure, or too far from your life. That is allowed. A book of this kind is not a test. If a day did not speak to you, nothing has gone wrong. Leave it, and take what did.
A last word

Thoreau died in 1862, at 44, and the essay reached readers after him. It ends with a hope and not a promise: that one day the light will shine “into our minds and hearts”. He could not say when, and we cannot either. What a road can do is smaller and surer. It gives you a long afternoon, a direction and a reason to look up.

If you are at the sea, look at it once more before you go. If you are at home, find the west on the next clear evening, and go and stand where you can see the sky. Then walk again, next year if you can, or tomorrow, around the block, with the phone left behind.
Buen Camino.
